deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. This page continues the previous one. The equations of motion are 0 = x'' + Θx/r^3 + X, with X = μ((x−x')/ρ^3 + x'/r'^3), and similarly for y and z. Here ⊙ = Θ = k^2 (mass factor absorbed). Note that (X,Y,Z) is MINUS the perturbing acceleration of the disturbing body (mass μ, position r'). On the previous page Gauss had the polar form of these equations in s = r cos b, λ and θ = tan b, and from it the variations di and dΩ. On this page he obtains dp, rewrites everything with the perturbed orbit's own plane as reference plane, derives d(1/a), defines force components T, V, W, and lists the variations of i, Ω, p, a and φ (e = sin φ). In modern terms these are Gauss's planetary equations. They serve his method for planetary perturbations (Pallas, c. 1810–13).

(a) dv = cos^2 b dλ / cos i. Areal velocity in the orbit plane, r^2 dv, projects onto the fundamental plane as s^2 dλ = r^2 cos i dv. Hence dv = (s/r)^2 dλ / cos i.

(b) √p = s^2 dλ / (cos i · k dt). This follows from r^2 dv/dt = k√p.

(c) Differentiate s^2 λ' = k√p cos i in time.
- The second polar equation s λ'' + 2 s' λ' = X sinλ − Y cosλ gives d(s^2 λ') = s (X sinλ − Y cosλ) dt.
- So k cos i d√p − k√p sin i di = s (X sinλ − Y cosλ) dt.
- Multiply by dt/cos i and use k√p dt = s^2 dλ / cos i: k dt d√p = (s dt^2/cos i)(X sinλ − Y cosλ) + s^2 tan i dλ di / cos i. This is the page's formula.
- [My step] With x = s cosλ, y = s sinλ we get x sinλ − y cosλ = 0 and x' sinλ − y' cosλ = s' sin(λ−λ').
- Hence X sinλ − Y cosλ = μ s' (1/r'^3 − 1/ρ^3) sin(λ−λ'), the second line.

(d) 'Man sieht leicht dass die Fundamentalebene hier willkürlich ist.' Take the instantaneous plane of the perturbed orbit as reference plane. Then i = 0 there, s = r, λ = v, s' = r' cos β' and λ' = w', where w' and β' are the longitude and latitude of the disturbing planet referred to that plane.
- dp = 2√p d√p = 2μ r r' cos β' √p k dt/⊙ · (1/r'^3 − 1/ρ^3) sin(v − w'), using 1/k = k/⊙.
- di and dΩ: the bracket of the previous page, −X sin i sinΩ + Y sin i cosΩ − Z cos i, equals −(X·n), with n the orbit normal. It is therefore plane-independent and equals μ r' sin β' (1/ρ^3 − 1/r'^3).
- With cos i dt^2/(s dλ) = s dt/(k√p) and s cos(λ−Ω) = r cos(v−Ω), this gives di = μ r r' k dt cos(v−Ω)/(⊙√p) · (1/ρ^3 − 1/r'^3) sin β'.
- Likewise dΩ is the same with sin(v−Ω)/sin i in place of cos(v−Ω). Here i and Ω stay referred to an arbitrary fixed plane.

(e) Vis viva: 1/a = 2/r − (dx^2+dy^2+dz^2)/(⊙ dt^2).
- Differentiating along the perturbed motion gives d(1/a) = (2/⊙)(X dx + Y dy + Z dz).
- Expanding X: X·dr = μ[r dr/ρ^3 − (1/ρ^3 − 1/r'^3) d(r·r')], with only the perturbed coordinates varied.
- r·r' = r r' cos β' cos(v − w'), so d(r·r') = r' cos(v−w') cos β' dr − r r' sin(v−w') cos β' dv.
- Comparing with dp, the dv term equals −dv dp/(k dt √p).

(f) Definitions (the V and W lines are partly under the ink blot, but are fixed by results 1–3):
- T = (μ/⊙)[r/ρ^3 − (1/ρ^3 − 1/r'^3) r' cos(v−w') cos β'] = (X·r̂)/⊙.
- V = (μ/⊙)(1/ρ^3 − 1/r'^3) r r' sin(v−w') cos β' = r (X·t̂)/⊙, with t̂ transverse in the direction of motion.
- W = (μ/⊙)(1/ρ^3 − 1/r'^3) r r' sin β' = −r (X·n)/⊙.
- So T is a force component, while V and W are moments (r times force). Then d(1/a) = 2(T dr + V dv).

Marginal box:
- d(1/a) = (2μ/⊙) dR, with R = ξ/r'^2 − 1/ρ and ξ = r·r'/r'. Then μ dR = X·dr, so R is minus the usual disturbing function divided by μ.
- 'dμ = (3μ/⊙) a μ dR', where the second μ is the mean motion. This follows from dn/n = (3/2) a d(1/a).

(g) The list:
- 1) di = (k dt/√p) W cos(v−Ω).
- 2) dΩ = k dt W sin(v−Ω)/(sin i √p).
- 3) dp = −2√p k dt V.
- 4) da = −a^2 d(1/a) = −2a^2 (T dr + V dv). [Mine] Using dr/dt = k e sin(v−ω)/√p and dv/dt = k√p/r^2: da = −(2a^2 k dt/√p) T e sin(v−ω) − (2a^2 √p k dt/r^2) V.
- 5) [Mine] From p = a cos^2 φ and e = sin φ: dφ = (cos^2 φ da − dp)/(2a sinφ cosφ). This yields dφ = −√a k dt T sin(v−ω) − [2cos(v−ω) + e + e cos^2(v−ω)]/(cos φ √p) · k dt V.
- 5) second form: −√a k dt T sin(v−ω) − (√a/r) k dt (cos f + cos E) V, with f = v−ω the true anomaly (written 'cos v') and E the eccentric anomaly. It uses cos E = (e + cos f)/(1 + e cos f).

(h) NB: dv has been used in two senses, as the differential of the orbital longitude v and as the element of heliocentric motion. The next page separates them: dv = dϖ + (1 − cos i) dΩ. That correction enters the formulas for dω and dε.
errors: No substantive mathematical errors found; every displayed formula checks.

Sign conventions are mixed but consistent with the stated definitions. (X,Y,Z) is minus the perturbing acceleration, so T = −F_r/k^2, V = −r F_t/k^2 and W = +r F_n/k^2. The results 1)–5) carry signs consistent with these definitions.
Notational overloading: μ denotes the disturbing mass and, in 'dμ = 3μ/⊙ · aμ · dR', also the mean motion. In 5) the second line writes cos v for the true anomaly v−ω.
Gauss himself flags the conceptual slip at the end: dv is conflated with the in-orbit element of motion. This is harmless for p, a, φ, i and Ω, but matters for ω and ε (fixed on the next page).
In the d(1/a) chain, d(xx'+yy'+zz') must be read as a partial differential (perturbed coordinates only). This is implicit but correct.

results.what: Areal relations dv = cos^2 b dλ/cos i and √p = s^2 dλ/(k cos i dt), and the time derivative of √p in projected polar coordinates.
results.usually_credited_to: Kepler/Newton (area law); standard 18th-century celestial mechanics (Euler, Lagrange, Laplace)

results.what: Variations of p, i, Ω in terms of disturbing-force components, with the instantaneous orbit plane as reference plane: dp = −2√p k dt V, di = k dt W cos u/√p, dΩ = k dt W sin u/(sin i √p).
results.modern_name: Gauss's form of the planetary equations (Gauss variational equations, RSW/RTN components)
results.usually_credited_to: Euler and Lagrange for early versions; the force-component form is standardly named after Gauss (Pallas work c. 1810–1813; 'Exposition d'une nouvelle méthode de calculer les perturbations planétaires', Werke VII)

results.what: d(1/a) = (2/k^2) X·dr = 2(T dr + V dv), and da = −2a^2[T e sin f k dt/√p + V √p k dt/r^2]; dn = (3/k^2) μ a n dR.
results.modern_name: Energy (vis-viva) form of the semimajor-axis equation in Gauss's planetary equations
results.usually_credited_to: Lagrange/Laplace (vis viva, da/dt = 2a^2 ∂R/∂ε); Gauss for the component form

results.what: Eccentricity-angle equation: dφ = −√a k dt T sin f − (√a/r)(cos f + cos E) k dt V.
results.modern_name: de/dt in Gauss's planetary equations: de/dt = √(p/μ)[F_r sin f + F_t (cos f + cos E)]
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (classical form); appears in standard texts (e.g. Brouwer–Clemence, Danby)

results.what: Observation that the fundamental plane is arbitrary and the perturbed orbit's own plane can be used, giving the components through w' and β'.
results.modern_name: Use of osculating-orbit (RSW) frame for perturbing force
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss / standard practice from early 19th century

deep.surprise_reason: This is a working draft of Gauss's own form of the planetary perturbation equations in radial/transverse/normal components. That form is already attributed to Gauss through his Pallas perturbation work (Werke VII). The page is a correct and careful derivation, but it contains nothing beyond what is known as his.

cos f + cos E = (2cos f + e + e cos^2 f)/(1 + e cos f); the two forms of formula 5) agree. Should give 0.

transcription_corrections: The symbol written ⊙ (Sun sign) is the same as Θ = k^2 of the previous page. In the T line the image shows μ/⊙ (the transcription's own T line already reads μ/⊙; the faint sign could be misread as μ/φ).
The V and W lines are partly obscured by the ink blot; the '[?]' can be removed. Results 1)–3) confirm V = (μ/⊙)(1/ρ^3 − 1/r'^3) r r' sin(v−w') cos β' and W = (μ/⊙)(1/ρ^3 − 1/r'^3) r r' sin β'.
In 5) the numerator is 2cos(v−ω) + e + e cos(v−ω)^2, i.e. cos^2(v−ω); the '[?]' marks can be dropped.
In the second line of 5) the coefficient is √a/r (the written symbol may look like '2√a'); 'cos v' there means the true anomaly v−ω.
In the last d(1/a) line the first term reads r/ρ^3 (overwritten from r∂r/ρ^3), multiplied by ∂r outside the bracket.
Margin: R = ξ/(r'r') − 1/ρ, with ξ = r cos(angular distance) as on the next page. 'dμ' uses μ for the mean motion.
